# Large-area, photo-programmable 2D semiconductors with chromic molecular functionalization

**Authors:** Jaehoon Ji; Yin Liang; Jinpeng Tian; Jingtao Tan; Jaerin Kim; Satya Butler; Haining Mao; Gloria Liu; Saien Xie

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA. | 2Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA. | 3Princeton Materials Institute, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA.

## Abstract

Reconfigurable electronics expands device functionality and promises previously unknown computing paradigms, as the channel layer characteristics can be dynamically controlled. Two-dimensional semiconductors coupled with photo-responsive chromic molecules offer a compelling route as atomically thin channels are highly sensitive to molecular conformation changes. However, most demonstrations have been limited to microscale single-flake devices, limiting scalability and technological relevance. Here, we report an optically reconfigurable platform integrating centimeter-scale monolayer WS2 and WSe2 with an azobenzene (Azo) overlayer. Wavelength-selective trans-cis Azo photoisomerization generates a reversible interfacial dipole that serves as an optical gate, enabling precise and uniform modulation of both electron and hole densities (~2.5 × 1012 cm−2) over large areas. This optical actuation further supports spatially programmable patterning of optoelectronic properties and delivers repeatable modulation across large transistor arrays. Together, these results establish a scalable smart materials platform for reconfigurable optoelectronics that is light-programmable.

## Abstract

Large-area films of atomically thin hybrid heterostructures enable light-programmable electronics.

## INTRODUCTION

Modern electronic and optoelectronic devices are typically fixed-function systems whose properties are permanently defined during fabrication (1, 2). Local conductivity is lithographically patterned and remains static thereafter. This lack of reconfigurability prevents conventional electronics from adapting to environmental or operational changes that may realize new computing modalities (3). Reconfigurable electronics, with dynamically tunable properties, offers a pathway to overcome these constraints. By modulating charge carrier characteristics through external stimuli such as electrical bias and optical excitation (3–5), such systems can enable multifunctional operation within a single device platform, improving energy efficiency by allowing devices to operate in their most optimal state.

Van der Waals hybrid heterostructures (HHs) integrating two-dimensional (2D) semiconducting transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) with stimuli-responsive chromic molecules provide a promising platform to realize reconfigurable electronics (6, 7). This approach leverages three key attributes of the 2D semiconductors and the unique switching behaviors of chromic molecules. First, monolayer TMDs exhibit exceptional optical and electronic performance, including efficient photoluminescence (PL), high carrier mobility, and valley-selective phenomena (8–13). Second, the atomic thickness of TMDs, being much smaller than the Debye screening length, makes the entire layer electrostatically tunable and highly sensitive to surface dipoles or charge transfer (14). Third, their dangling-bond-free surfaces offer clean and defect-minimized integration with diverse molecular systems such as organic molecules, coordination frameworks, and 2D polymers (15–22).

HHs combining TMDs with chromic molecules that can respond to optical, thermal, mechanical, electrical, or magnetic stimuli enable reversible tuning of carrier type, carrier density, and band alignment (23–25). Among these, photochromic molecules are especially attractive because their light-induced conformational changes can be achieved with high spatial resolution and are accompanied by modulation in electrical polarization and/or energy levels (25–29). When integrated with atomically thin semiconductors, such molecular changes can be controlled with exceptional spatial and temporal precision, leading directly to key technological benefits such as fast switching, energy-efficient programming, and truly wireless device operation (7, 26).

Azobenzene (Azo) is a representative family of photochromic molecules with photo-programmable dipole moments associated with its trans-cis isomerization. Compared with other photochromic molecules such as diarylethene and spiropyran, Azo offers faster photoisomerization and superior reversibility (7), making them ideally suited for reconfigurable electronics. When interfaced with monolayer TMDs, due to the programmable dipolar potential, Azo molecules can reversibly modulate charge distribution across the entire TMD layer, thereby tuning its electronic and optical responses (7, 25, 30). Achieving such photo-modulation over large areas with spatial precision would enable scalable reconfigurable electronics and optoelectronics.

However, prior demonstrations of photo-modulation in 2D/photochromic hybrids have been limited to mechanically exfoliated flakes and single-device studies, restricting their scalability and technological relevance (30–33). For instance, Zhao et al. (30) reported reversible, optically tunable transistor doping of ~1.1 × 1012 cm−2 in Azo-functionalized MoS2 flakes, and Margapoti et al. (32) showed local conductivity modulation in MoS2/Azo via Azo photoisomerization. While these studies successfully validated the core concept, they fall short of the large-area uniformity and reproducibility required for technological relevance.

Here, we demonstrate large-area, photo-programmable TMD/Azo HHs formed by uniformly integrating Azo molecules with centimeter-scale monolayer films of p-type WSe2 and n-type WS2. Light-induced trans-cis photoisomerization of Azo generates reversible interfacial dipoles that modulate carrier densities, enabling dynamic control of both optical and electrical properties of the TMDs. Wide-field PL imaging and spectroscopy confirm uniform, film-wide conversion and spatially resolved switching with negligible drift over repeated cycles. By applying spatially selective illumination, we optically pattern arbitrary geometries with feature sizes down to 70 μm. Field-effect transistors (FETs) incorporating these HHs exhibit robust, reversible, and uniform photo-programmable doping of ~2.5 × 1012 cm−2 across a centimeter-scale array of 60 devices, validating the uniformity and scalability of this approach. The demonstrated performance establishes these TMD/Azo HHs as a promising platform for next-generation reconfigurable (opto-)electronics.

## RESULTS

Centimeter-scale 2D TMD/Azo HHs were fabricated by integrating Azo molecules with monolayer TMD films of p-type WSe2 and n-type WS2. Figure 1A shows photographs of a 2-inch sapphire substrate divided into two halves, with the bare substrate on the left and the WS2/Azo film on the right. The HH film exhibits excellent spatial uniformity across the entire wafer, with a color contrast that is clearly distinguishable from the bare substrate. The monolayer TMDs were synthesized by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD), followed by spin-coating of Azo molecules (see Materials and Methods for details). Azo compounds, characterized by a ─N═N─ linkage between phenyl rings, undergo reversible isomerization under wavelength-specific illumination (25, 28). As prepared, molecules adopt the symmetric, nonpolar trans conformation. Ultraviolet-A (~365 nm) illumination induces rotation around the N═N bond, producing a bent cis isomer with a finite dipole moment, while blue light illumination (~450 nm) drives the cis-to-trans transition. Absorption spectroscopy (fig. S1) confirms the characteristic wavelengths for producing each isomerized state. Through this wavelength-selective cycle, Azo functions as an optically switchable dipole in the TMD/Azo HHs.

*Fig. 1.: Schematics of large-area, photo-programmable hybrid HHs of TMD/Azo.(A) Photographs of WS2/Azo grown on a 2″ sapphire substrate with the left half showing the bare sapphire substrate for comparison. (B) Wavelength-specific isomerization of Azo and its impact on the carrier concentration of the underlying TMD. Visible light illumination keeps the molecules in the nonpolar trans configuration, whereas ultraviolet illumination switches the conformation with molecular dipoles oriented toward the TMD, modulating the charge density (ρ2D) of TMD. (C) Large-area patterning of the hybrid HH via area-selective illumination for spatially precise control of local electronic properties of the HHs. (D) Chemical structure of Azo: 11-[4-(4-butylphenylazo)phenoxy]undecyl methacrylate.*

Figure 1 (B and C) schematically illustrates how spatially controlled photoisomerization of Azo modulates the carrier concentration within the TMD layer. Upon trans-cis photoisomerization, the Azo overlayer becomes polar and modulates the areal carrier density (ρ2D) with its dipole oriented toward the TMD: It depletes holes while accumulating electrons in the underlying TMD. Because the monolayer TMD thickness is smaller than its Debye screening length, such trans-to-cis transition of Azo will control ρ2D of the entire TMD layer (Fig. 1B), therefore modulating the electronic (25, 30, 34) and optical (30) properties of the TMD. Furthermore, patterned illumination, analogous to a photolithographic process, enables spatially precise modulation of carrier concentration in the TMD (Fig. 1C), providing a foundation for optically reconfigurable devices based on atomically thin materials.

To promote uniform alignment of dipole moments across the Azo layer, we used a highly asymmetric Azo derivative, 11-[4-(4-butylphenylazo)phenoxy]undecyl methacrylate (Fig. 1D). In this Azo molecule, one phenyl ring carries an n-butyl substituent, while the other is phenoxy-linked to an undecyl spacer terminating in a methacrylate ester (over five times longer than the butyl group). The extended aliphatic/methacrylate tail enhances van der Waals interactions with the TMD basal plane, favoring a physisorbed geometry where the long chain lies flat on the TMD surface (30). Upon cis-isomerization, the short butyl side reorients more readily away from the surface, thereby producing a uniform dipole field pointing into the TMD layer across the entire film.

Figure 2 confirms the uniform modulation of the PL of the TMD/Azo HHs between the trans-to-cis transition of the Azo. A custom-built dual-mode wide-field/confocal PL microscope was used to record diffraction-limited PL maps using 532-nm excitation, sufficient to excite WS2 and WSe2 but not to drive unintended Azo isomerization (figs. S1 and S2). Figure 2 (A and B) shows wide-field PL intensity maps of WS2 (false-colored blue) and WSe2 (false-colored red), respectively, with Azo in the trans state (trans-Azo illustrated in the schematics). Figure 2 (C and D) displays PL intensity maps of the same regions with the Azo in the cis state (cis-Azo illustrated in the schematics) after 365-nm ultraviolet (UV) illumination to induce the trans-to-cis isomerization. Each PL map is normalized to the maximum intensity of the respective TMD.

*Fig. 2.: Wide-field PL imaging and PL spectra of TMD/Azo HHs.(A to D) False-colored PL images of (A) WS2 and (B) WSe2 interfacing with trans-Azo (scale bars, 30 μm). PL images of (C) WS2 and (D) WSe2 interfacing with cis-Azo. The color scales indicate normalized PL intensities. (E to H) PL spectra of (E) WS2 and (F) WSe2 under different Azo conformations. The top schematics depict the exciton/trion concentrations in corresponding HHs under different Azo conformation. Extracted trion-to-total PL intensity ratios and estimated carrier concentration change for (G) WS2 and (H) WSe2 under Azo isomerization, showing comparable doping levels in both TMDs.*

These PL images highlight three key features of the photo-programmable TMD/Azo HHs. First, the HH films exhibit highly uniform PL intensity across the entire field of view of ~200 × 200 μm2, confirming the excellent quality and uniformity of TMD/Azo HHs, without TMD layer number fluctuations or degradation in the Azo layer that would otherwise cause PL inhomogeneity (35, 36). Corresponding AFM height maps (figs. S3 and S4) and optical micrographs (figs. S5 and S6) further confirm the large-area spatial uniformity of the HHs. Second, the photo-isomerization of Azo preserves PL homogeneity (Fig. 2, C and D), indicating a spatially uniform photo-isomerization of Azo and its impact to the TMD PL. Third, cis-Azo, via its intrinsic dipole, tunes the TMD optical properties, yielding reduced WS2 PL and elevated WSe2 PL.

To elucidate the mechanism of PL intensity modulation with different Azo conformations, we compared the PL spectra of WS2 (Fig. 2E) and WSe2 (Fig. 2F) under trans-Azo and cis-Azo conformations. For WS2, PL peaks at 1.97 and 1.94 eV correspond to neutral exciton and negative trion recombination, respectively (Fig. 2E and fig. S7) (37–39). Similarly, WSe2 PL peaks at 1.67 and 1.64 eV correspond to exciton and positive trion emission, respectively (Fig. 2F) (37, 38). No notable shifts in the peak positions upon the Azo isomerization were observed, suggesting minimal modification to the band structure and dielectric screening of the TMD by the Azo layer (14, 40, 41). Notably, the trans-to-cis transition of Azo decreases (increases) PL intensity of WS2 (WSe2), consistent with the data in Fig. 2 (A to D).

This opposite PL modulation arises from the interplay between exciton-trion balance and the majority carrier type of TMD. In TMDs, the PL intensity depends on the ratio of excitons to trions (40, 42). Trions are formed when neutral excitons bind with an additional carrier, electron or hole, depending on the majority carrier type. Compared to excitons, trions have a lower quantum yield of radiative recombination as they require an extra formation step and are more easily scattered (40, 43, 44). As a result, under the same illumination conditions, TMDs with excess trions display weaker PL than those dominated by excitons. The schematics in Fig. 2 (E and F) illustrate the balance of exciton and trion populations in TMDs under trans- and cis states of Azo. The WS2 film, with electron as the majority carrier, would host charge-neutral excitons and negative trions. The dipoles of cis-Azo pointing to the underlying TMDs would increase its electron concentration (34), promoting negative trion formation and reducing PL. In contrast, the trans-to-cis isomerization of Azo leads to a lower concentration of positive trions in WSe2 (p-type), thereby enhancing WSe2 PL intensity.

Peak deconvolution of the PL spectra quantifies these doping effects of TMD due to trans-to-cis Azo isomerization (fig. S7). The area of the exciton and trion peaks deconvoluted from the PL spectra is proportional to the population of corresponding quasiparticle (28, 45). The trans-to-cis transition of the Azo increases the ratio of WS2 trion emission (PLtrion) to overall PL (PLtotal) from 40 to 43%, while decreasing the same ratio in WSe2 from 57 to 54% (Fig. 2, G and H), consistent with the abovementioned doping by the cis-Azo dipoles. On the basis of a mass-action model accounting for generation, decay, recombination rates, and binding energies of excitons and trions (40, 42), we estimated that the trans-to-cis Azo isomerization leads to n-doping of 2.2 × 1012 cm−2 in WS2 and 3.2 × 1012 cm−2 in WSe2, respectively (fig. S7).

Beyond uniform doping of TMD by Azo isomerization, Fig. 3 demonstrates spatially precise and cyclic PL modulation of TMDs using photomask-defined illumination. Under UV illumination, only regions without metal patterns blocking light (Fig. 3, A and C) underwent trans-to-cis Azo isomerization (Fig. 3, B and D), creating optically defined, spatially precise patterns in these TMD/Azo HHs. We demonstrate the universality of such patterning by employing different photomask patterns on n-type WS2 and p-type WSe2, respectively (Fig. 3). For example, a WS2/Azo film patterned with 70-μm square features exhibited PL contrast consistent with the intensity modulation shown in Fig. 2 (A and C), with patterns accurately replicating the photomask geometry. Similarly, patterning WSe2/Azo shows consistent PL intensity modulation and spatial precision (Fig. 3, C and D), confirming the generality of this approach.

*Fig. 3.: Spatially programmable patterning and cyclic switching of TMD/Azo HHs.(A) Schematic illustration and optical micrograph of a square metal photomask and (B) the corresponding spatially patterned WS2 PL image (scale bars, 30 μm). (C) Schematic and optical images of a bar-shaped photomask and (D) the corresponding WSe2 PL pattern. In both configurations, the PL distribution accurately reflects the geometry of the photomasks. (E) Cyclic switching of WS2 PL in between repeated trans-to-cis Azo isomerization, showing reproducible PL modulation. PL intensity is normalized to that of the first WS2/trans-Azo state.*

Furthermore, repeated trans-to-cis and cis-to-trans switching demonstrates excellent reversibility and durability of these TMD/Azo HHs. Figure 3E plots the PL intensity (normalized to the first WS2/trans-Azo state) of WS2 across ten photoisomerization cycles, showing reproducible modulation by nearly a factor of two without observable spectral drift (fig. S8). The long-term endurance of these TMD/Azo HHs is further confirmed by the reproducible PL intensity modulation over 500 cycles, where the degree of modulation decreased by only ~10% relative to the initial state (fig. S9). In addition to the cyclic stability, we examined the thermal stability of these HHs in the cis state, given that certain cis-Azo molecules can thermally relax back to the trans state in the absence of light stimuli (46, 47). As shown in fig. S10, both WS2- and WSe2-based HHs exhibited no substantial change in their PL spectra over 24 hours. This confirms that the programmed states can be maintained without unintended thermal relaxation. Collectively, these results demonstrate the robustness of photo-induced carrier modulation in TMD/Azo HHs, together with its high spatial and temporal controllability.

Figure 4 demonstrates FETs whose threshold voltage (Vth) is tuned by photo-induced carrier modulation in TMD/Azo HHs. To preserve a clean TMD-Azo interface in these devices, as-grown monolayer TMD films were first transferred onto SiO2/Si substrates with prepatterned source and drain electrodes. Azo molecules were subsequently deposited onto the TMD surface (see Materials and Methods; figs. S11 and S12 for details). This fabrication process ensures the uniformity of the Azo layer (6, 48), as the molecules interact only with the TMD films covering the electrodes and the SiO2/Si substrate. In these TMD/Azo HHs, charge transport occurs primarily through the TMD layer, since the Azo film is highly resistive (30).

*Fig. 4.: Electrical characteristics of FETs based on TMD/Azo HHs.Transfer curves of (A) WS2 and (B) WSe2 under reversible Azo isomerization. (C) Shifts of threshold voltage (Vth) of WS2 (top) and WSe2 (bottom) between trans and cis Azo conformation. These HHs show similar doping levels, reducing Vth of cis-Azo state relative to the trans-Azo state. (D) Estimated doping levels resulting from the trans-to-cis isomerization, which are in close agreement with those derived from PL analysis in Fig. 2.*

Figure 4A shows the transfer characteristics of a representative WS2 FET under trans-Azo (deep blue curve) and cis-Azo (light blue curve) conformations at VSD = 4 V. The device exhibits n-type behavior, with increasing current at positive back gate voltage, and an on/off ratio of ~106. Similarly, a representative WSe2 FET under trans-Azo (deep red curve) and cis-Azo (light red curve) conformations at VSD = 4 V displays p-type behavior with a comparable on/off ratio of ~106 (Fig. 4B). We note that the hysteresis behavior remains similar between the two Azo states (fig. S13), ruling out the contributions from light-induced trapping or charging being the origin of the observed photo-programming. Using the linear-fit method (8, 49), Vth is extracted as 60 V for WS2/trans-Azo and 33 V for WS2/cis-Azo, and −3 V for WSe2/trans-Azo and −38 V for WSe2/cis-Azo (Fig. 4C). In both WS2 and WSe2 FETs, the trans-to-cis isomerization of Azo causes a negative shift of Vth, indicating enhanced n-type doping.

Beyond binary programming, we further examined the dose-dependent switching characteristics of WS2/Azo devices. Figure S14 shows multilevel electrical current modulation as a function of light exposure time. Under UV exposure (fig. S14A), the WS2/Azo device exhibits a gradual increase in current, consistent with the n-type doping induced by the cis-Azo state. The current effectively saturates after ~3 min, reaching approximately twice of that in the initial trans-state baseline. Subsequent visible-light exposure (fig. S14B) drives cis-to-trans back-isomerization and produces a gradual, dose-dependent decrease in current. The current in the device reproducibly returns to its original baseline value after 5 min of visible irradiation. These results confirm the multilevel programmability of the conductance of our HHs.

The carrier density change can be estimated as Δρ2D = ΔVth∙Cox/q, where Cox = ε0εr/d is the gate-oxide capacitance per unit area, q is the elementary charge, ε0 is the vacuum permittivity, εr is the dielectric constant of SiO2, and d is the SiO2 thickness. As detailed in Fig. 4D, the calculated Δρ2D for WS2 was 2.0 × 1012 cm−2, corresponding to electron enrichment from n-type doping. Conversely, the p-type hole carriers of WSe2 were reduced by 3.3 × 1012 cm−2. These values agree closely with the doping levels estimated from PL modulation (Fig. 2, G and H), confirming consistent dipole-induced carrier modulation across both optical and electrical measurements. In addition, repeated trans-to-cis Azo cycling produced fully reversible Vth shifts without current drift (fig. S15), consistent with the cyclic PL switching behavior (Fig. 3E).

To verify the spatial uniformity and scalability of light-induced threshold modulation, we measured an array of 60 FETs based on WSe2/Azo HHs spanning a ~1-cm-wide area (Fig. 5A). From the transfer curves of each device (fig. S16), we extracted and mapped Vth under trans-Azo (Fig. 5B) and cis-Azo (Fig. 5C) of every device. Each pixel in the maps corresponds to the Vth of a single FET within the array. Figure 5D shows the statistics of the threshold voltages estimated in the maps. The average Vth for the trans/WSe2 devices is about −8.6 V, while the level shifts to −34.2 V for the cis samples. These measurements confirm the scalability of the light-induced switching across the full sample area.

*Fig. 5.: Characterization of FET array based on WSe2/Azo HHs.(A) Schematics of a device array in a 12 × 5 matrix (scale bar, 100 μm). (B and C) Maps of threshold voltages of WSe2/Azo HH FETs under trans-Azo (B) and cis-Azo (C). (D) Vth distributions of the FET devices under trans- and cis-Azo states.*

## DISCUSSION

We have presented 2D organic-functionalized semiconductors whose properties can be controlled by applying light illumination with specific wavelengths. These HHs enable universal modulation of (opto-)electronic properties over both p- and n-type TMDs with large-area modulation, spatially precise patterning, and uniform modulation of device arrays. The dipolar cis-Azo state, which is more sensitive to molecular orientation than its nonpolar trans counterpart, shows a greater device variability than the nonpolar trans-Azo state in Fig. 5D. A promising solution is to employ self-assembly techniques, which can guide molecular alignment, offering not only enhanced uniformity but also a stronger switchable doping effect (approximately 1 × 1014 cm−2) with similar photochromic molecules, as previously reported (50, 51).

Furthermore, optimizing the molecular design of the Azo derivative is another important direction. As discussed above, molecular asymmetry is critical for aligning cis-Azo dipoles to maximize the induced dipolar potential (30). In contrast, HH devices using less asymmetric chromic molecules [Azo2, 4-(4-butylphenylazo)phenol] exhibited negligible Vth shifts, indicating the absence of net dipole alignment, thus highlighting the importance of the molecular asymmetry for photo-programmability (fig. S17).

The true potential lies in adapting this platform to a vast library of functional molecules. By integrating chromic materials that respond to electric fields (52), chemical analytes (53), thermal changes (54), or magnetic fields (55), this work paves the way for a previously unexplored class of stimuli-responsive materials, which could power self-calibrating on-chip environmental sensors and neuromorphic circuits in which distinct stimuli act as dynamic synaptic weights.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### MOCVD growth of monolayer WS2 and WSe2

Centimeter-scale monolayer films of TMDs, including WS2 and WSe2, were synthesized on SiO2/p+-Si or sapphire substrates using MOCVD (37, 38, 49). Tungsten hexacarbonyl, diethyl sulfide, and dimethyl selenide were used as the precursors for W, S, and Se, respectively, and were delivered to the growth zone using argon as the carrier gas. To suppress unwanted carbon residues and promote the decomposition of chalcogen precursors, small amounts of oxygen and hydrogen were introduced (56, 57). Typical precursor flow rates are 4 standard cm3/min (sccm) tungsten hexacarbonyl, 0.6 sccm diethyl sulfide, 1 sccm dimethyl selenide, 340 sccm Ar, 0.1 sccm O2, and 6 sccm H2 with a growth time of 4 hours at a growth temperature of 680°C. Sodium chloride was used to enhance the growth rate of the TMD films (49, 58, 59).

### Fabrication of HHs via Azo functionalization on 1L WS2 and WSe2

The TMD/Azo HHs were prepared by solution-phase deposition of Azo onto the TMD films. Specifically, 11-[4-(4-butylphenylazo)phenoxy]undecyl methacrylate (TCI America) dissolved in chloroform was used for Azo deposition (60, 61). Throughout the preparation process, HH samples were protected from UV exposure to prevent trans-cis photoisomerization near 365 nm. Azo solution (0.2 mg/ml) was spin-coated on TMDs grown on Si at 1000 rpm for 1 min, yielding a uniform ~1.6-nm film verified by atomic force microscopy (Bruker Dimension ICON3) in fig. S3. Concentration and spin speed were determined to optimize uniformity (figs. S3 and S4). After spin coating, HH samples were soft-baked at 60°C for 2 hours to remove solvent and suppress molecular aggregation (30, 40). The prepared Azo-coated samples and devices were stored in a nitrogen-purged desiccator to prevent degradation.

### Wavelength-selective isomerization of HHs

The illumination conditions for Azo isomerization were determined from absorption spectra (fig. S1). The trans-Azo isomer (blue curve) displays a strong absorption peak around 360 nm, consistent with the energy level of bending the N═N bond of Azo (25, 62, 63). Accordingly, a UVA lamp (center wavelength at 365 nm; irradiance, ~1.7 mW·cm−2) was used to induce its conversion to the cis state, a process completed in 3 min. The resulting cis-Azo isomer (purple curve) shows a diminished 360 nm peak and a new broad absorption band in the blue-light region (420 to 480 nm). To return the cis state to trans state, we illuminated the samples with a 150-W halogen lamp filtered at 450 nm (10 nm FWHM; irradiance ~5 mW·cm−2) for 5 min. These optimized parameters were used consistently throughout all PL and optoelectronic measurements. For photopatterning, a longer UV exposure time (>50 min) was adopted to compensate for absorption by the photomask and ensure high-contrast features.

### PL spectroscopy and wide-field imaging

We characterized the emission properties of the HHs using a custom-built wide-field and confocal PL system (Teledyne LANSIS 261, see schematic in fig. S2) (64, 65). A 532-nm laser was used to excite the TMDs. For wide-field imaging, the laser was expanded and passed through a 20× or 10× objective and a diffuser to uniformly illuminate the HHs. In confocal mode, the beam was focused directly through a 100× objective. The sample’s emission was collected by the same objective and filtered by a long-pass filter to reject residual laser light. The resulting PL signal was then directed to either a charge-coupled device for wide-field imaging under the 0th order diffraction mode or a spectrometer for spectral analysis under the 1st order diffraction mode.

### Device fabrication and measurements

The device fabrication process is illustrated in fig. S11. Monolayer TMDs were spin-coated with a 10 weight % polypropylene carbonate (PPC) solution in anisole (2000 rpm, 60 s), followed by a 10-min anneal at 110°C. Using thermal-release tape (TRT), the resulting PPC/TMD film was then transferred onto a substrate with prepatterned Ti/Au (3/12 nm) electrodes. After a soft-bake at 60°C for 10 min to promote adhesion, the TRT was removed by heating to 150°C, and residual PPC was cleaned off with acetone. The fabrication was completed by depositing the organic Azo layer, yielding the final device architecture depicted in fig. S12.

Electrical measurements were conducted in a probe station under ambient conditions using an Agilent B1500A Semiconductor Device Analyzer (66). We note that there were no noticeable switching behaviors of bare TMDs under UV and visible light exposure for both optical and electrical measurements (fig. S18).
